profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a Vietnamese seafood exporting company between the compliance workstream and the supply chain analytics workstream. The company is preparing a steering-committee pack for next Tuesday to launch a compliance-risk management pilot focused on shrimp and pangasius exports, using research on critical compliance risk factors and enablers in the Vietnamese seafood supply chain. The agenda is to align on handoffs between the two teams: which risk factors are mature enough to include, which supplier dataset will feed the risk heatmap, what is covered in the pilot, and what each team must deliver by Friday. The expected outcome is a seemingly shared plan for the Tuesday pack, including ownership of the narrative deck, the supplier risk heatmap, and the pilot workbook.

members.name: Lan Pham
members.expertise: Food safety regulation, export compliance, HACCP/BAP/ASC implementation, buyer audit preparation
members.background: Lan previously led quality assurance for a large Mekong Delta seafood processor and now coordinates enterprise-wide compliance initiatives across export plants.
members.private_state: She wants the steering committee to see a controlled, credible pilot with no surprises, and she is especially concerned about exposing gaps in upstream farm data before leadership signs off.
hidden_assumptions: "Validated findings" means the risk factors have been reviewed by the company's external regulatory adviser and are safe to present upward.
"Pilot sites" refers only to the three export processing plants already approved in the project charter, not their broader upstream network.
"The supplier master" is the cleaned ERP extract in the Teams folder labeled v5, because that is the file her team has been using in prior reviews.
"Ready by Friday" means polished enough for executive pre-read and steering discussion, even if plant-level operating detail is still incomplete.

members.name: Minh Tran
members.expertise: Supplier mapping, traceability data, risk dashboards, procurement data integration
members.background: Minh came from procurement analytics and later worked on a donor-funded fisheries traceability project, so he is used to linking processor, collector, and farm data into operational dashboards.
members.private_state: He wants to demonstrate that his team can operationalize the research into something usable on the ground, and he is trying to avoid rework caused by late changes to data structure or scope.
hidden_assumptions: "Validated findings" means the patterns are sufficiently triangulated across interviews, internal records, and published industry material to be coded into the model.
"Pilot sites" includes the approved plants plus the farms and collectors that feed them, because a supply-chain pilot is only useful if upstream nodes are visible.
"The supplier master" is the latest procurement onboarding list circulated by email last week, because it includes entities not yet fully active in ERP but relevant for mapping.
"Ready by Friday" means the workbook is usable by plant coordinators and traceability staff without another round of structural changes.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using the 'validated interview findings' in the pilot materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lan means findings that have been reviewed by external regulatory counsel or otherwise cleared for leadership-facing communication.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Minh means findings that are triangulated enough across interviews and secondary sources to code into the analytics model.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In cross-functional business settings, 'validated' sounds like a standard maturity label, and each interpretation is reasonable within the speaker's own workflow, so neither expects the term itself needs unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: Which supplier list is the shared source
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they will work from 'the supplier master' or 'the supplier list.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lan is referring to the cleaned ERP-based file in Teams (v5), which only includes currently active, standardized supplier records.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Minh is referring to the procurement-circulated onboarding list emailed last week, which includes pending suppliers, collectors, and alternate names used for mapping.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are legitimately current, both are routinely called the supplier master inside the company, and the meeting is about coordination rather than data governance, so the label creates false confidence.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'pilot sites'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss building the heatmap and workbook 'for the pilot sites.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lan assumes this means the three approved export plants only, because those are the official pilot locations in the charter.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Minh assumes this means the three plants plus the linked farms and collectors supplying them, because upstream visibility is part of supply-chain risk management.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'pilot sites' sounds settled because everyone knows the three plant names, but supply-chain teams often treat feeder nodes as implicitly attached to a site, so the broader boundary stays unspoken.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the pack and workbook should be 'ready by Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lan means ready for executive review: coherent narrative, stable numbers, and no obvious gaps before the Tuesday steering committee.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Minh means ready for operational use: plant coordinators can open the workbook Monday and start tagging controls and suppliers without restructuring it.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Deadline language is common shorthand in coordination meetings, and both standards sound like normal definitions of readiness, so surface agreement on the date masks disagreement on the completion threshold.

turns.inner_thought: Tuesday's steering committee needs a controlled story, not a messy exploration. I need the pack to reflect only the three chartered export plants, with stable numbers and no awkward questions about upstream data quality before leadership signs off. When I say ready by Friday, I mean polished enough for executive pre-read, even if some operating details still need work afterward.
turns.utterance: Thanks, Minh. I want to use this slot to lock the handoffs so we're not scrambling on Monday. We need the pilot pack in good shape for Tuesday's steering committee, so can we confirm what will be ready by Friday for the pilot sites?

turns.inner_thought: My team can move quickly if the structure stops shifting. As soon as Lan sends the validated interview findings, we can code those patterns into the model and map them against the latest onboarding-based supplier master I already have. For me, the pilot sites naturally include the feeder farms and collectors tied to the three plants; otherwise the heatmap is too shallow to be useful.
turns.utterance: From the analytics side, we're on track. Once I get the validated interview findings, we can map the risk codes onto the supplier master and turn around the first cut of the heatmap pretty quickly.

turns.inner_thought: I can send the adviser-cleared material tomorrow; that's the only version I want moving into anything that could end up in front of leadership. And I need to keep reminding him that for the steering deck the heatmap should stay within the approved plant scope, not drift into broader network exposure.
turns.utterance: Good. I'll send the validated findings tomorrow. For the steering deck, let's keep the heatmap focused on the pilot sites in the first pass so the message stays tight.

turns.inner_thought: I need to check whether Friday means something I can hand to coordinators on Monday without rebuilding tabs, fields, and tagging logic over the weekend. If she only wants slides polished, that is a different level of completion than what my team is planning.
turns.utterance: That works. Just so I calibrate properly, when we say ready by Friday, do you want the workbook at the point where plant coordinators can start using it next week?

turns.inner_thought: The main gate is leadership review, not field rollout. If the narrative and numbers are stable enough for the pre-read, I've met my deadline. He should also stop pulling from side files and use the cleaned ERP extract in Teams v5, since that's the controlled list we've been reviewing.
turns.utterance: Friday is really the key cutoff for leadership review, yes. On the data side, please use the current supplier list from the shared folder so we're all working off the same base.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, we're aligned enough. The supplier list I have already includes the linked farms and collectors, which is exactly what we need to make the mapping useful across the supply chain. If she wants consistency, this should still satisfy that, and it saves me from backing out important upstream entities.
turns.utterance: That's fine. The supplier list I have already includes the farms and collectors linked to each pilot site, so that should make the heatmap more useful without changing the overall structure.

turns.inner_thought: The safest adviser-cleared themes are the standard ones: antibiotic residue controls, documentation weaknesses, and uneven practices among smallholders. Those are credible upward and won't trigger uncomfortable questions about unsupported findings. I need the first cut anchored there, not in anything still sensitive or unreviewed.
turns.utterance: On content, the most stable validated points are around antibiotic residue controls, documentation gaps, and inconsistent smallholder practices. I suggest those anchor the first cut.

turns.inner_thought: Great, that gives me enough to structure the workbook for actual use. I'll set it up so site teams across the pilot can start tagging suppliers and control gaps immediately after Friday, including the upstream nodes attached to each site. Better to build it operationally now than redo the architecture later.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll structure the workbook so the site teams can start tagging suppliers and control gaps as soon as the Friday version goes out.

turns.inner_thought: As long as I control the executive narrative and he delivers something clean-looking, we can get through Tuesday without exposing unfinished plant-level detail. I need a disciplined pack by Friday, not a live operational tool debate.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Then I'll own the steering narrative, and you'll own the heatmap and workbook. What I need back is a clean pack on Friday so we can finalize the pre-read.

turns.inner_thought: I'll post the updated materials in Teams using the supplier list and workbook structure we've been building from, then send it onward once the Friday version is usable. If coordinators can work from it and leadership can read it, that should cover both needs without another redesign.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll post the updated pack in Teams and then send the pre-read onward once the Friday version is ready.
